title: When You Report to an Idiot
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece offers blunt, tactical advice for managing up when your boss lacks the intelligence and experience for the role. It first concedes that leaving for another team or organisation is a reasonable choice, then turns to how to make the best of the situation if a move is impractical. Its central move is to recast an incompetent leader's cluelessness as a source of latitude: because such leaders rarely know what is going on, the subordinate can act on their own judgment and explain later. The piece pairs that freedom with a reciprocal obligation to learn what matters to the boss and make them look good, which earns still more autonomy. It then gives specific influence tactics, such as appealing to emotion rather than logic, explaining how people will feel about a decision, and framing choices around risks and rewards instead of data. It closes with a wry line reminding readers to bring the crayons.
points: The piece treats leaving as a legitimate option, but gives a survival playbook for those who conclude a move is impractical.
An incompetent boss's lack of awareness is reframed as an opportunity for autonomy, with the working rule of asking forgiveness rather than permission.
Autonomy is bought by finding out what matters to the leader and making those things happen in a way that makes them look good.
To persuade such a leader, appeal to emotion and to how people will feel, and focus on risks and rewards rather than data they cannot process.
quotes: Deciding to find another team or place to ply your craft is not an unreasonable call. But if you conclude that a move is impractical then you need to make the best of a bad situation.

Idiot leaders generally lack the intelligence and experience to do the job. They have a hard time processing complex information and are easily confused by anything not straightforward or black and white.
Instead of waiting for the next moronic decision, enjoy the freedom to do largely what you want. Do it your way and explain yourself later.
Be sure to go out of your way and find out what is important to them. Work hard to make those things happen and to make them look good in the process. More freedom to do what you want is your reward.
When engaging them, appeal to emotion, not logic. To sway their choices and decisions, explain to them how people will feel about matters.

Try not to overwhelm them with information or data they can’t make sense of. Instead, focus their attention on the risks and rewards involved with any decision. This is what they will find most persuasive.
